lines: A two-position switch putting out a steady 0V or 10V by hand, with a text area for writing down what it is patched to
Puts out 0V in one position and 10V in the other
Carries 0V or 10V, following the switch
Note — the dark area on the panel takes typed text, for labelling what the switch controls; the text is saved with the patch
Note — shift-dragging up or down on the module name changes the colour of the panel, and holding ctrl as well makes the change finer
A button putting out 10V while it is pressed and 0V the rest of the time, with a text area for writing down what it is patched to
Puts out 10V for as long as it is held down
Carries 10V while the button is held and 0V otherwise
Note — the dark area on the panel takes typed text, for labelling what the button controls; the text is saved with the patch
Note — shift-dragging up or down on the module name changes the colour of the panel, and holding ctrl as well makes the change finer
Four sliders, each putting out a steady voltage from 0V to 10V, with a text area for writing down what they are patched to
Sets the voltage at the output of the matching letter, 0V at the bottom of its travel and 10V at the top
Carries the voltage set by the slider of the matching letter, 0V to 10V
Note — the dark area on the panel takes typed text, for labelling the four sliders; the text is saved with the patch
Note — shift-dragging up or down on the module name changes the colour of the panel, and holding ctrl as well makes the change finer
A knob putting out a steady voltage from -5V to 5V, with a text area for writing down what it is patched to
Sets the output voltage: -5V fully counter-clockwise, 0V at noon and 5V fully clockwise
Carries the voltage set by the knob, -5V to 5V
Note — the dark area on the panel takes typed text, for labelling what the knob controls; the text is saved with the patch
Note — shift-dragging up or down on the module name changes the colour of the panel, and holding ctrl as well makes the change finer
A knob putting out a steady voltage from 0V to 10V, with a text area for writing down what it is patched to
Sets the output voltage: 0V fully counter-clockwise and 10V fully clockwise
Carries the voltage set by the knob, 0V to 10V
Note — the dark area on the panel takes typed text, for labelling what the knob controls; the text is saved with the patch
Note — shift-dragging up or down on the module name changes the colour of the panel, and holding ctrl as well makes the change finer
A reverb built on the GVerb code, taking mono or stereo audio and returning stereo, with a CV input and an attenuverter for every control; the maker calls it dirty and unstable
Sets the size of the modelled room in metres, 2 to 300, which sets the length of the longest delay inside the reverb
Sets how fast the tail loses its high frequencies, 0 for none and 1 for the most, starting at 0.98
Sets how long the tail takes to decay, 0 to 10 seconds
Sets how much of the input's high end reaches the reverb, 1 passing the signal whole and 0 filtering it heavily; it starts at 0.01
Sets the level of the early reflections in the reverb signal, 0 to 1
Sets the level of the reverb tail in the reverb signal, 0 to 1
Crossfades the output between the dry input at 0 and the reverb alone at 1
Sets how far apart the two output channels are, mixing them to mono at 0 and leaving them separate at 1; the reverb engine's own spread stays fixed at 90 degrees
Rebuilds the reverb engine from scratch, clearing whatever it was doing; the knob settings are left alone
Attenuates and inverts the CV going to ROOM SIZE, -1 to +1, and at zero that CV changes nothing
Attenuates and inverts the CV going to DAMP, -1 to +1, and at zero that CV changes nothing
Attenuates and inverts the CV going to TIME, -1 to +1, and at zero that CV changes nothing
Attenuates and inverts the CV going to BANDWIDTH, -1 to +1, and at zero that CV changes nothing
Attenuates and inverts the CV going to EARLY, -1 to +1, and at zero that CV changes nothing
Attenuates and inverts the CV going to LATE, -1 to +1, and at zero that CV changes nothing
Attenuates and inverts the CV going to MIX, -1 to +1, and at zero that CV changes nothing
Attenuates and inverts the CV going to SPREAD, -1 to +1, and at zero that CV changes nothing
Modulates the room size; 10V through the ROOM attenuverter at +1 adds 300 metres to the knob setting, and the result is clamped to 2 to 300 metres
Modulates the damping; 10V through the DAMP attenuverter at +1 adds 1 to the knob setting, and the result is clamped to 0 to 1
Modulates the decay; 10V through the TIME attenuverter at +1 adds 10 seconds to the knob setting, and the result is clamped to 0 to 10 seconds
Modulates the input bandwidth; 10V through the BW attenuverter at +1 adds 1 to the knob setting, and the result is clamped to 0 to 1
Modulates the early reflection level; 10V through the EARLY attenuverter at +1 adds 1 to the knob setting, and the result is clamped to 0 to 1
Modulates the tail level; 10V through the LATE attenuverter at +1 adds 1 to the knob setting, and the result is clamped to 0 to 1
Modulates the dry and reverb balance; 10V through the MIX attenuverter at +1 adds 1 to the knob setting, and the result is clamped to 0 to 1
Modulates the channel separation; 10V through the SPREAD attenuverter at +1 adds 1 to the knob setting, and the result is clamped to 0 to 1
A rising edge rebuilds the reverb engine from scratch, clearing whatever it was doing
The left audio input; a reverb engine for this channel exists only while a cable is patched here, and unpatching the cable throws that engine away
The right audio input; a reverb engine for this channel exists only while a cable is patched here, and unpatching the cable throws that engine away
The left output, crossfading dry against reverb according to MIX; with nothing patched to the left input the dry part comes from the right input
The right output, crossfading dry against reverb according to MIX; with nothing patched to the right input the dry part comes from the left input
Note — an envelope follower inside the module divides both outputs down whenever the reverb climbs past 10V, which can pull the level about on its own during loud passages
Note — the reverb engine is built when a cable is patched to an audio input and thrown away when that cable is removed; with nothing patched to either input both outputs are held at 0V
Note — shift-dragging up or down on the module name changes the colour of the panel, and holding ctrl as well makes the change finer
rcm-gverb.notes: Panel lettering differs from the code names: the panel prints TIME for what the code calls reverb time and LATE for what it calls tail level. The lines use the panel's words. One oddity in the code: when a reverb engine is first built, the decay CV is scaled by 10000 rather than the 10 used from then on, so a decay CV present at the moment a cable is patched in can set an extreme first value.

lines: Fades one pair of audio inputs down under another pair whenever that other pair makes a sound, in mono or stereo
Sets how hard the over signal pushes the under signal down, 0 for no ducking at all and 2 for the hardest; the setting is squared before it multiplies the detected level
Sets how slowly the ducking lets go once the over signal falls away, as a time constant from 0 to 1 second
The left channel of the audio that takes priority; the louder of the two over channels drives the ducking, and this signal crossfades into the left output
The right channel of the audio that takes priority; the louder of the two over channels drives the ducking, and this signal crossfades into the right output
The left channel of the audio pushed down, which crossfades out of the left output as the ducking deepens
The right channel of the audio pushed down, which crossfades out of the right output as the ducking deepens
Crossfades between the left under input and the left over input, moving towards the over input as the ducking deepens
Crossfades between the right under input and the right over input, moving towards the over input as the ducking deepens
Note — nothing is normalled between the two sides; a mono source patched to the left OVER and left UNDER inputs comes back at the left output, and the right output stays at 0V
Note — shift-dragging up or down on the module name changes the colour of the panel, and holding ctrl as well makes the change finer
rcm-duck.notes: RECOVERY divides by the setting, so at 0 the recovery time is zero and the detected level follows the over signal instantly. The over channels are mixed into the output as well as driving the detector, so this is not a sidechain-only ducker.

lines: Retimes the run, reset and clock coming from a clock module so that a simple sequencer sounds its first step when the clock is started again after a reset
A reset arriving while the module counts itself stopped arms it rather than being passed on; a reset arriving while it counts itself running goes straight to the RESET output
Each trigger here flips the module between running and stopped
Passes straight to the CLOCK output; while the module is armed the next pulse is copied to the RESET output as well, and two pulses arriving while the module counts itself stopped set it running
Carries the reset for the sequencer: the incoming reset while running, or a copy of the first clock pulse after a reset arrived with the clock stopped. It holds 0V while the module is stopped
Carries the clock input unchanged
Note — the green lamp shows the module's own idea of whether the clock is running, and the yellow lamp shows that the next clock pulse will be copied to the RESET output
Note — the module comes up counting itself stopped, and while it counts itself stopped the RESET output is held at 0V
Note — it starts running on a trigger at RUN, or after two clock pulses have arrived with no reset between them
Note — shift-dragging up or down on the module name changes the colour of the panel, and holding ctrl as well makes the change finer
rcm-seq-adapter.notes: A RUN output is declared in the code and carries the run input, but no jack for it is placed on the panel, so it cannot be clicked and has no line. With Impromptu's Clocked, the maker recommends turning off its 'Outputs reset high when not running' option.

lines: Holds an incoming reset back until the next clock pulse, so that a sequencer restarts in step with the rest of the patch
The clock pulse; it passes through to the CLK output, and a reset being held is released the moment a pulse arrives here
A reset arriving while the clock input is at 0V is held until the next clock pulse; one arriving while the clock input is above 0V goes out at once
Carries the clock input unchanged, unless No CLK on Reset is turned on, in which case it holds 0V from the reset pulse until the next clock pulse arrives
A 10V pulse carrying the reset, timed to land with a clock pulse
Menu — No CLK on Reset — holds the CLK output at 0V while a reset pulse is going out, for sequencers such as SS-1 and SS-2 that misread a clock and a reset arriving together
Note — the green lamp follows the clock input and the yellow lamp shows a reset being held back for the next clock pulse
Note — a reset that arrives while the clock input is at 0V is held until a clock pulse arrives at CLK, so with no clock patched there a held reset never reaches the RESET output
Note — shift-dragging up or down on the module name changes the colour of the panel, and holding ctrl as well makes the change finer
Puts out white noise on as many polyphonic channels as the cable patched into it carries
Only the number of polyphonic channels is read here, not the signal itself; with nothing patched, one channel of noise comes out
White noise between -5V and 5V, a separate stream on every channel
Note — shift-dragging up or down on the module name changes the colour of the panel, and holding ctrl as well makes the change finer
rcm-polynos.notes: The SRC input has no family: anything at all can be patched there, because only its channel count is used.

lines: A monophonic step sequencer programmed on a piano roll grid, holding 64 patterns of up to 16 measures, with pitch, gate, retrigger and velocity outputs and inputs for recording into the grid
Each rising edge advances the sequence by one division; pulses arriving while the module is paused are ignored, and there is no internal clock
A trigger sets the play position back to the start of the pattern, so that the next clock pulse plays the first note
Selects the pattern by pitch: 0V picks the first of the 64 and every semitone above that picks the next one
Each trigger flips the sequence between running and paused, without reading whether the clock is actually running
A trigger arms recording, which begins when the play position wraps round to the start of the pattern; a second trigger cancels the arming or stops the recording
The pitch written into the step being played while recording, quantised to the nearest semitone
A level above 1V while recording makes the step being played sound, and a level below 0.1V at the start of a step silences it
A level above 1V while recording marks the step being played to retrigger, and a level below 0.1V at the start of a step clears that mark
Sets the velocity written into the step being played while recording, 0-10V mapped onto the step's own 0 to 1 velocity
Carries the clock input unchanged, for chaining the clock on to another piano roll
Carries the reset input unchanged, for chaining the reset on to another piano roll
The pattern now selected, as a pitch: 0V for the first and a twelfth of a volt for each one after, rather than the copy of the PTRN input the manual describes
Carries the run input unchanged, for chaining the run signal on to another piano roll
Carries the record input unchanged, for chaining the record signal on to another piano roll
The pitch of the step now playing, 0V for C4 and a twelfth of a volt per semitone; while a gate above 1V is present at GATE the unquantised 1V/OCT input comes out here instead
10V while the step now playing sounds. With nothing patched to RTRG it drops to 0V for 1ms where a retrigger falls, and with nothing patched to RUN a gate lasts at most 2 seconds
A 1ms 10V pulse at the start of a step that follows a silent step, and at the start of any step marked to retrigger
The velocity of the step now playing, 0-10V
A 1ms 10V pulse when the last step of the pattern has been played
Note — left-clicking a cell in the grid makes that note sound, right-clicking an active note marks it to retrigger, and shift-dragging a note up or down sets its velocity
Note — clicking the strip above the grid moves the play position and sounds the note there, and dragging across it plays along
Note — clicking the strip below the grid picks the measure; holding on a measure for a second loops that measure alone, and holding again releases it
Note — the readouts beside the grid are clicked with the left button, not the right, and each opens its own list
Note — the pattern readout steps down or up when clicked at its ends, and opens a list of the 64 patterns when clicked in its middle
Note — the readouts under the pattern number open lists headed Measures, Beats Per Measure and Divisions Per Beat, 1 to 16 of each
Note — the bottom readout beside the grid shows whether the sequence is running, paused or recording, and clicking it starts or pauses it
Note — the pattern readout ignores clicks while a cable is patched to PTRN, because the pattern is then chosen by that input
Menu — Copy Pattern — copies the pattern now selected; a Paste Pattern item then appears in the same menu and writes the copy over whatever pattern is selected when you click it
Menu — Copy Measure — copies the measure now selected; a Paste Measure item then appears in the same menu and writes the copy over whatever measure is selected when you click it
Menu — Clear Notes — empties every note in the pattern now selected
Menu — Notes to Show — a heading over the choices 12, 18, 24, 36, 48 and 60, setting how many rows of the grid are drawn
Menu — Clock Delay (samples) — a heading over the choices 0, 1, 2, 3, 4, 5 and 10, holding the clock input back by that many samples so a pattern change can arrive first
Menu — Driver Mode — makes a run or reset signal pick the first step at once rather than waiting for a clock pulse, so a piano roll driving another selects the pattern first
Note — a new Piano Roll has an empty grid and plays nothing until notes are put into it by left-clicking cells, or recorded through the record inputs
Note — the module has no clock of its own; nothing advances until a clock is patched to CLOCK
Note — shift-dragging up or down on the module name changes the colour of the panel, and holding ctrl as well makes the change finer
rcm-pianoroll.notes: Two params, the run and reset buttons, are declared in the code but no widget is placed for either, so neither can be clicked and neither gets a line. The grid, the play-position strip, the measure strip and the pattern panel are all drawn inside custom widgets with no ParamWidget of their own, so they cannot be clicked for help either; they are covered by Note lines. The PTRN output is not a copy of the PTRN input, as the README says the left outputs are, but the currently selected pattern expressed as a pitch.
